newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela bolivar seen as achilles heel of reforms.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela bolivar seen as achilles heel of reforms.

text.p: Increasing bolivar strength is the Achilles' heel of Venezuela's economic reform program, according to some economists attending a conference here.
They said over-valuation could threaten a foreign exchange market meltdown next year.
"Next year the exchange market will be more complex, more fragile than this year," Bear Sterns emerging markets executive director Tulio Vera told conference delegates Tuesday.
"In the medium term, over-valuation of the bolivar could imperil the exchange rate mechanism."
Vera put current bolivar over-valuation at 10-15 percent, as did SBC Warburg's Director of Economic Studies Walter Molano.
But not all economists at the "Wall Street's view of Venezuela" conference agreed that the bolivar was dangerously over-valued -- at least not yet.
"If you use labor costs to calculate the real exchange rate, the bolivar is still not over-valued," Credit Suisse First Boston's Latin American Emerging Markets director Javier Murcio said.

Venezuela has used a strong bolivar to bear down on domestic inflation since price and foreign exchange controls were removed in April last year. Despite inflation that has nudged 100 percent, the exchange rate has hardly moved in 12 months.
But growing fiscal pressure in 1998 could nevertheless prompt a devaluation, Murcio said.
Devaluations boost the government's bolivar revenues from Venezuela's dollar-denominated oil exports.

"This year's fiscal balance is assured on oil windfalls, but that won't be around in 1998...If government revenues are short (then) and the bolivar is strong, well Wall Street has a very mechanistic view about this kind of thing," he added.
Government officials have said they expect to end 1997 with a fiscal surplus equivalent to 1.6 percent of gross domestic product.
Despite the mid-term uncertainties, SBC Warburg's Molano said he saw Venezuela becoming "one of the region's lest risky and most important markets."
Investment house Santander also forecasts an 84 percent real return from the stock market over the next 18 months.
